title: The Accidental HR Manager: How Rural California Employers Can Avoid 3 Costly Compliance Traps
author: Brynn Fogerty
tags: Siskiyou County HR consultant, California small business HR compliance, fractional HR Northern California
excerpt: Practical guidance for rural California employers on employee exemptions, outdated handbooks, and documenting workplace conversations.
body:
If you run a small business, a medical practice, a non-profit, or a local district here in Siskiyou County, there's a good chance nobody on your team has "HR" in their job title. Instead, HR is one of five hats worn by the owner, or the office manager who already keeps everything else running.

We call this person the Accidental HR Manager. They didn't go to school for California labor law, but they're suddenly responsible for handbooks, break schedules, leave requests, and the hard conversations nobody wants to have. If that's you, this article is for you.

The Reality of Managing People in Siskiyou County

Most rural organizations with 10 to 100 employees simply can't justify a $110,000–$140,000 salary for a full-time HR Director. That's a reasonable business decision. The challenge is that California doesn't scale its employment laws down for small employers. The same wage-and-hour rules, leave requirements, and training mandates that apply to a Bay Area tech company apply to a family-owned hardware store in Yreka.

Add in the dynamics of a small town -where your employee may also be your neighbor, your kid's coach, or someone you'll see at the grocery store on Saturday -and workplace issues carry a weight that generic, big-city HR advice rarely accounts for.

After two decades working with Northern California employers, I see the same three traps over and over. The good news: each one is fixable, usually without much cost, once you know what to look for.

Trap #1: Assuming a Salary Makes Someone Exempt

This is the single most expensive mistake I see small employers make. A trusted lead or supervisor gets moved to a flat salary -often as a sign of respect, or so nobody has to track their hours -and everyone assumes overtime no longer applies.

In California, salary alone does not make an employee exempt. To be exempt from overtime and meal-and-rest-break rules, an employee generally must pass two tests:

  • The salary test: earn at least twice the state minimum wage for full-time work. In 2026, that's at least $70,304 per year. Careful, minimum wage is increasing January 1, 2027, so this amount will increase to $72,384 per year.
  • The duties test: spend more than 50% of their actual working time on genuinely exempt work -managing, exercising independent judgment, or performing professional duties.

If your crew lead spends most of the day doing the same hands-on work as the crew, they likely fail the duties test -no matter what you pay them. That can mean years of back overtime, missed meal-period premiums, and penalties.

Job titles do not matter. Just because you give someone a fancy title such as manager or supervisor, it doesn’t mean they are automatically exempt. The state evaluates the actual day-to-day tasks.

The fix

  • List every salaried employee and what they actually do in a typical week.
  • Compare their real duties -not their job title -against the 50% rule.
  • Reclassify where needed and get advice on how to handle any past exposure.

Trap #2: The Dust-Covered Template Handbook

Many small employers have a handbook they downloaded, inherited, or adapted from a national template years ago. It feels like protection. In California, it can quietly become a liability.

California employment law changes nearly every legislative session. In just the past few years, employers have had to account for expanded paid sick leave, reproductive loss leave, workplace violence prevention plans, and updated rules on cannabis use and off-duty conduct. A generic federal template doesn't cover any of that -and a handbook that contradicts current law can be used against you. Did you have AI write your handbook? AI often doesn’t write complete policies which you need to reduce liability and protect your business.

Your handbook doesn't need to be 100 pages of corporate jargon. It does need to reflect current California law and how your organization actually operates.

The fix

  • Check the date: if your handbook is more than two years old, it needs review.
  • Confirm your sick leave, leave-of-absence, and meal/rest break policies match current law.
  • Make sure every employee signs an acknowledgment of the current version.

Trap #3: Handshake Discipline

This one shows up most in close-knit communities. Having a tough conversation with someone you've known for years is uncomfortable, so managers drop gentle hints and hope things improve.

Sometimes they do. But when they don't -and you eventually need to let that person go -there's no record showing what was expected, what was discussed, or what chances they were given. That's exactly the situation that turns a reasonable decision into a wrongful-termination or retaliation claim.

If it isn't written down, it didn't happen. Clear, compassionate documentation isn't cold or corporate. It's fair to your employees, because they know where they stand, and it protects your business if a dispute ever arises.

The fix

  • After any performance conversation, write a short, dated note: the issue, the expectation, and the timeline.
  • Share expectations with the employee in writing and keep a copy in their file.
  • Be consistent -treat similar situations the same way across your team.

A Smarter Model: Fractional HR

You don't need a full-time HR department to have great HR practices. Fractional HR gives small employers access to experienced HR leadership -handbook audits, compliance reviews, on-call advice for tricky employee situations -for a few hundred dollars a month instead of a six-figure salary.

It's the support your Accidental HR Manager needs to stop guessing and start operating with confidence.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do small businesses in California have to follow the same labor laws as large companies?

Mostly, yes. Wage-and-hour rules, overtime, meal and rest breaks, and paid sick leave apply regardless of size. A few requirements, like harassment prevention training, begin at five employees.

How often should a California employee handbook be updated?

At least once a year. California passes new employment laws almost every session, most taking effect January 1.

What is a fractional HR consultant?

An experienced HR professional who supports your organization part-time or on retainer, providing expert guidance without the cost of a full-time hire.
